hints.text: Who should bring the torch back each time?
Send the two slowest across together, so 8 minutes pays for both.
1 and 3 cross, 1 returns, 6 and 8 cross, 3 returns, 1 and 3 cross: $3 + 1 + 8 + 3 + 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair the two slowest, and keep the fast pair for the returns.

explain.text: 1 and 3 cross, 1 returns, 6 and 8 cross, 3 returns, and 1 and 3 cross. That costs $3 + 1 + 8 + 3 + 3 = 18$. The 8-minute walker carries the 6-minute walker for free.

screens.title: A different four
screens.prose: Now the four take 1, 4, 5 and 6 minutes. Two plans move the two slowest. The fastest escorts each in turn, or the two fastest shuttle the torch.

state.caption: Each trip costs the slower walker's time.

screens.question: What is the fewest minutes for 1, 4, 5 and 6?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the escort plan as well as the shuttle.

byKey.shuttle: The shuttle costs 19 here: the 4-minute walker returns, which is dear.
byKey.sum: That adds the three slowest; someone must also bring the torch back twice.

explain.text: Escorting costs $4 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 6 = 17$ and shuttling $4 + 1 + 6 + 4 + 4 = 19$. Here the second-fastest is slow, so his return trip is too dear. A search over every plan confirms 17.

screens.title: Three burgers
screens.prose: A grill holds two burgers, and each side takes 4 minutes. You must cook both sides of three burgers, A, B and C. A burger can come off and go back on.

state.caption: Two places on the grill, 4 minutes a slot.

screens.question: What is the fewest minutes to cook all three?

hints.text: Count the sides and the places.
Six sides, two at a time, 4 minutes each.
$6 \times 4 / 2 = 12$, and it is reachable: A2 with C1, then B2 with C2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count six sides and two places, then find a schedule.

byKey.sixteen: You finished A and B first, leaving C alone on the grill for 8 minutes with a place empty.
byKey.eight: Eight minutes cook only four sides; there are six.

explain.text: Six sides at two a slot need at least three slots of 4 minutes: 12. Cook A1 and B1, then A2 and C1, then B2 and C2. Principle: count the work against the capacity, then fill every slot.

screens.title: The fastest escorts
screens.prose: Back to 1, 3, 6 and 8. A candidate reasons that the fastest should walk everyone over and bring the torch back each time.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes for 1, 3, 6 and 8?

options.why: You let the fastest escort everyone. Sending 6 and 8 together saves their separate trips.
Nothing beats 18: a case check on whether 6 and 8 cross together rules it out.
Pairs walk at the slower pace, so the faster partner crosses free.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair the two slowest instead of escorting each.

byKey.19: Escorting pays 8 and 6 separately. Pairing them pays 8 once and costs one extra 3-minute return.
byKey.17: Seventeen is impossible here; the shuttle's 18 is the best.
byKey.21: Each pair walks at its slower member's pace, not their sum.

explain.text: Escorting pays 8 and 6 separately: $8 + 1 + 6 + 1 + 3 = 19$. Sending 6 and 8 together pays 8 once, at the cost of a 3-minute return: 18. Principle: let the slowest share a trip.

screens.title: Nothing beats 18
screens.prose: Prove that 1, 3, 6 and 8 need 18 minutes. A plan has at least three trips over and two back. A search of every plan shows that more trips cost more. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the proof.

lines.text: With three trips over and two back, each trip over carries two people.
Case 1: 6 and 8 cross on different trips, costing at least $8 + 6$.
The third trip over costs at least 3 and each return at least 1: at least 19.
Case 2: 6 and 8 cross together, costing 8, and neither walks back.
The other trips over are both 1 and 3, costing 3 each, and 1 and 3 make the returns: $1 + 3$.
So case 2 takes at least $8 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 18$, which the plan meets.
The fastest must escort each slow walker, so 19 is the floor.
lines.why: Escorting is one plan, not a bound. Sending 6 and 8 together beats it.

hints.text: Split on whether 6 and 8 cross together.
Together, the trips over cost $8 + 3 + 3$ and the returns $1 + 3$.

feedback.correct: Trips, case 1, case 2, and the matching plan.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the trips, then take the two cases in turn.

byKey.d1: A plan is not a proof. The case split shows 18 is the floor.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the escort claim belongs.

explain.text: Apart, 6 and 8 cost at least $8 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 19$. Together, the trips over cost $8 + 3 + 3$ and the returns, made by 1 and 3, cost 4: 18. Principle: split on how the two slowest cross.

screens.title: Two people
screens.prose: Edge case. Only two people need to cross, taking 3 and 8 minutes, with the same bridge and torch.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes?

hints.text: One trip at the slower pace: 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. They cross once, together, at the slower pace.

byKey.eleven: Pairs walk at the slower pace, not the sum.
byKey.fourteen: Nobody needs to bring the torch back once both are over.

explain.text: Both cross together in one trip, at the slower pace: 8 minutes. Nobody returns, since nobody is left. One person alone would take their own time.

screens.title: Escort or shuttle
screens.prose: Each time, we moved the two slowest by the cheaper pattern. With times $a \le b \le y \le z$: escort costs $z + a + y + a$; shuttle costs $b + a + z + b$. $$\text{shuttle when } 2b < a + y$$ For 1, 3, 6, 8: $6 < 7$, so shuttle. For 1, 4, 5, 6: $8 > 6$, so escort.
screens.question: Which pattern wins for 1, 3, 4 and 9?

options.why: $2b = 6$ is more than $a + y = 5$, so the returning 3 is too dear.
Escort costs 18 and shuttle 19, so they differ.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $2b = 6$ with $a + y = 5$.

explain.text: Here $2b = 6$ and $a + y = 1 + 4 = 5$, so escort wins. Escort costs $9 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 18$, shuttle 19. A search over every plan agrees.

screens.title: Drill: 2, 3, 8, 9
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Four people take 2, 3, 8 and 9 minutes, same bridge, same torch.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Here the shuttle wins by a lot.

byKey.sum: That adds all four; pairs walk at the slower pace.

explain.text: $2b = 6$ is less than $a + y = 10$, so shuttle. 2 and 3 cross, 2 returns, 8 and 9 cross, 3 returns, 2 and 3 cross: $3 + 2 + 9 + 3 + 3 = 20$. Principle: compare $2b$ with $a + y$.

screens.title: Drill: 1, 5, 6, 7
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Four people take 1, 5, 6 and 7 minutes, same bridge, same torch.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Here the fastest should escort.

byKey.eighteen: That is $5 + 6 + 7$, with no returns; the torch must come back twice.

explain.text: $2b = 10$ exceeds $a + y = 7$, so escort. The 1-minute walker takes each across and returns: $5 + 1 + 6 + 1 + 7 = 20$. A search confirms it.

screens.title: Drill: auditors and traders
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Three auditors and three traders must cross a river in a boat for two, which needs one rower. On either bank, traders may never outnumber auditors while any auditor stands there.
screens.question: What is the fewest one-way crossings?

hints.text: Write each state as auditors and traders on the start bank, and the boat's side.
Begin: two traders cross, one returns.
A search over every safe state finds 11 crossings.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Search the safe states; the middle needs an auditor and a trader to return together.

byKey.nine: No safe route of 9 exists. A search over every safe state gives 11.
byKey.five: Five crossings are three over and two back, moving at most 4 people net. Six must cross.
byKey.thirteen: Thirteen works, but a shorter route exists.

explain.text: Traders shuttle first, then two auditors cross, then an auditor and a trader return together. That trip is the key, and the rest mirrors the start. A search over every safe state gives 11 crossings, the fewest.

screens.title: Drill: five burgers
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Five burgers, a grill for two, 3 minutes a side.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes?

hints.text: Ten sides, two at a time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ten sides fill five slots of two.

byKey.eighteen: You finished burgers in pairs and left one place empty for the last burger.
byKey.thirty: That is one place at a time; the grill holds two.

explain.text: Ten sides at two a slot need five slots of 3 minutes: 15. Rotate so no slot has an empty place, as with three burgers. Principle: when the work divides evenly, the count is the answer.

screens.title: A fifth walker
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer adds a fifth person: times 1, 3, 6, 8 and 12. Move the two slowest by the cheaper pattern, then solve the three left. Trade allocation across a few channels is scheduled the same way.
screens.question: What is the fewest minutes?

hints.text: Shuttle: $3 + 1 + 12 + 3 = 19$, back to 1, 3 and 6 at the start.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the two slowest, then solve the three that remain.

byKey.thirty: Close. Shuttling 8 and 12 costs 19, then 1, 3, 6 cost 10.

explain.text: Shuttling 8 and 12 costs $3 + 1 + 12 + 3 = 19$ and leaves 1, 3 and 6 at the start with the torch. They take $3 + 1 + 6 = 10$. A search over every plan confirms $19 + 10 = 29$.

ideas: Write the trips, then move the two slowest by the cheaper of two patterns: escort or shuttle.
Shuttle when twice the second-fastest time is less than the fastest plus the second-slowest.
Prove the bound by cases on whether the two slowest cross together.

formula.name: Escort or shuttle
formula.note: Times $a \le b \le y \le z$; 1, 3, 6, 8 shuttle to 18.

summary.trap: Letting the fastest escort everyone gives 19 for 1, 3, 6 and 8; pairing the two slowest gives 18.

quiz.prose: Four people take 1, 2, 7 and 8 minutes to cross a bridge for two with one torch.
quiz.question: What is the fewest minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $2b$ with $a + y$.

explain.text: $2b = 4$ is far below $a + y = 8$, so shuttle: $2 + 1 + 8 + 2 + 2 = 15$. A search over every plan confirms it. The 7 rides with the 8 for free.

quiz.prose: Four burgers, a grill for three, 5 minutes a side.
quiz.question: What is the fewest minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Eight sides need three slots of three places.

byKey.ten: Two slots hold six sides, but there are eight.
byKey.twenty: Three slots are enough: A1 B1 C1, then A2 B2 D1, then C2 D2.

explain.text: Eight sides, three at a time, need $\lceil 8/3 \rceil = 3$ slots of 5 minutes. A1, B1 and C1; then A2, B2 and D1; then C2 and D2. So 15 minutes.

quiz.prose: In the 1, 3, 6, 8 crossing, the 3-minute walker returns once.
quiz.question: Why is that worth paying?

options.text: It lets 6 and 8 cross together, so 6 costs nothing
The 3-minute walker is faster than the 1
options.why: The 1 is faster; the 3 returns because the 1 is on the other side.

options.text: Every plan must use each person to return
options.why: No such rule: the escort plan never sends 3 back.

feedback.correct: It lets 6 and 8 share a trip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the extra 3 minutes buy.

byKey.faster: The 1 is the fastest; the 3 returns only because he is where the torch is.

explain.text: Pairing 6 with 8 saves the 6 minutes of a separate trip. The price is a 3-minute return instead of a 1-minute one, 2 minutes more. Net, 18 beats 19.
